newsitem.title: USA: Delta seen flying solo for near-term.
newsitem.headline: Delta seen flying solo for near-term.

text.p: The pending resignation of Delta Air Lines Inc Chairman Ronald Allen has stirred speculation that Delta may renew merger talks with Continental Airlines Inc, but analysts expect Delta to fly solo -- at least for now.

"If you look at all possibilities out there, Delta and Continental make great dance partners ... but there's no reason to upset the apple cart at this point," said Edward Starkman, an airline analyst with Dillon Read.
"If a whole wave of merger activity started, Continental and Delta would be a good fit. But there's nothing imminent," Starkman said.
In an interview on CNBC Wednesday, Continental Chairman Gordon Bethune said his company is not in merger talks with any airline, "nor do we see any need to be."
Bethune also said he had not been contacted by Delta about succeeding Allen.
Allen will step down as chairman, chief executive and president when his employment contract ends July 31, according to a statement released by the company on Monday.
Delta said it would look both inside and outside the company for a successor.
Finding a replacement for Allen and overseeing product and service improvements are far bigger priorities for Delta than pursuing a merger, analysts said.

Delta has been through a painful restructuring in recent years but has cleared the most difficult hurdles. The final piece of the restructuring is currently under way as the airline improves its transatlantic service.
Analysts say Delta made a deliberate effort in its press release to stress that the "board intends for Delta to maintain its strategy of disciplined internal growth."

Delta and Continental abandoned short-lived merger talks last December. Some industry experts said the talks were cut off after Delta decided the deal offered insufficient financial benefits, analysts said.

A merger with Houston-based Continental would allow Delta to vacate Dallas-Fort Worth, where it has downsized in recent years. A deal would also give Delta access to Continental's strength in Latin and Central America.
In return, Delta would offer its strength in the U.S. Southeast and along the East Coast.
Since the good fit will remain in place for the foreseeable future, there's no urgency for Delta to rush into a merger, analysts said.

Delta is well-position with record profits and the recent success of its Delta Express unit, launched last autumn. Delta Express has allowed the airline to better compete against low-cost rivals such as Soutwest Airlines Co.

In a meeting with analysts Tuesday, Allen offered no explanation about why he is leaving Delta when the airline is so prosperous. He merely referred analysts to the company press release and called Delta "a wonderful place," analysts said.

Several analysts suspect Allen fell out of favor with Delta's board after several small incidents, including his attempted ouster of Chief Financial Officer Thomas Roeck and the pace of improvement in transatlantic service.
Although each problem separately was not a significant reason to push Allen out, collectively they caused the board to lessen its support for him, analysts said.
Analysts also suspect Allen may not have communicated enough with the board during the merger talks with Continental.
((--Jessica Hall, New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610))
